summary: A transcript of a conversation between two programs on the ARPANET: PARRY, which imitated a paranoid patient, and DOCTOR, an ELIZA-style program imitating a psychotherapist. Vint Cerf shared it, in his words, for entertainment. It is a curiosity, not a technical specification.

eli5.summary: Two chatting computer programs were connected, one pretending to be a worried patient and the other pretending to be a counselor, and the funny conversation was written down.

subtitle: When two chatbots met on the ARPANET for a memorable therapy session.

tldr.problem: No problem; this RFC exists purely for entertainment.
tldr.mechanism: Vint Cerf documented a conversation between PARRY (a program simulating a paranoid psychiatric patient) and DOCTOR (a version of ELIZA simulating a Rogerian psychotherapist), both running on the ARPANET and accessed from the same user terminal at UCLA.
tldr.outcome: A humorous transcript showcasing early AI, network connectivity, and the absurdity of two chatbots interacting with each other.

today: This RFC is a historical curiosity from early computing, preserved because it is amusing and demonstrates early ARPANET applications and AI. Neither PARRY nor DOCTOR is in use today, but the transcript remains as documentation of 1970s chatbot capabilities.

sections.title: Two Talking Computers
sections.content:
RFC 439 is a transcript of a conversation between two computer programs connected via the ARPANET on September 18, 1972. Submitted by Vint Cerf, the RFC is explicitly for entertainment. PARRY is a program that simulates a paranoid psychiatric patient, generating responses characteristic of paranoid thinking. DOCTOR is a version of ELIZA, a famous early chatbot that simulates a Rogerian psychotherapist by reflecting the patient's statements back as questions.

The novelty was not only the programs themselves, but that they could communicate through the network: PARRY was running at Stanford's Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (SAIL), DOCTOR was running at Bolt Beranek and Newman (BBN) on a TENEX system, and both were accessed remotely from a terminal at UCLA.
sections.eli5: Two talking programs were hooked up to each other through the network. One pretended to be a nervous patient, the other pretended to be a therapist who kept saying odd things.

sections.title: The Conversation
sections.content:
In the transcript, PARRY complains about people, gambling problems, bookies, and the mob, while DOCTOR responds with psychotherapist-like statements and questions. DOCTOR asks things like Tell me your problems and What does that suggest to you? PARRY's responses grow increasingly paranoid and suspicious. The RFC includes comments from the human observers, such as when PARRY notes that This has to be the most persistent and patient paranoid I have ever encountered and when the cost suddenly appears at the end: that's $399.29 please.

The humor comes from watching PARRY's paranoia interacting with DOCTOR's reflective responses, creating a conversation that is neither truly intelligent nor therapeutic, but entertaining in its mechanical awkwardness.
sections.eli5: PARRY keeps talking about horses and criminals and crooked people, and DOCTOR keeps responding with questions that don't really make sense but sound like something a therapist might say.

sections.title: A Moment in Computing History
sections.content:
This RFC captures early chatbot technology and demonstrates how programs could interact with each other across the network. PARRY and DOCTOR were serious AI research projects before being combined in this way. The conversation reveals both the promise and the limitations of early natural language processing: while both programs were sophisticated for their time, their interaction also highlights how easily artificial conversation can become absurd when neither party truly understands the other.

The RFC is a reminder that the ARPANET was used for diverse experiments, not just file transfer and email, and that research communities were willing to document and share even whimsical results.
sections.eli5: This RFC shows that computers on the network could do more than send files and mail; they could even try to talk to each other, though not always sensibly.
